basic_info.headline: MSc, MBA, MB (ASCP) | Bioinformatician
basic_info.about:
As a Bioinformatics Scientist at Tennessee Laboratory Services Department of Health, I apply my skills and knowledge in data science, molecular biology, and epidemiology to support public health initiatives and outbreak investigations. I have over 18 years of lab experience in clinical and molecular biology research and animal models, as well as a M.Sc. in Epidemiology with a focus on biostatistical analysis in epigenetics.

I am proficient in R, Python, Perl, and C++ programming, Linux platform, NGS analysis software tool kits, data analysis pipelines, and creation and development of SOPs. I also have multiple certifications in quality assessment of sequencing data and pathogen phylogenomics from CodeMode, a leading online platform for bioinformatics education. Additionally, I freelance as a consultant and content creator for scientific and educational materials, using white-hat SEO, Wordpress, and HTML scripts. My mission is to leverage bioinformatics to advance public health research and practice, and to share my expertise and passion with others.

projects.name: bioinfra-mlops-terraform
projects.description:
🌍 Bioinfra MLOps Mini Project — Terraform + MLflow + Multi-Cloud
This is a portfolio-ready mini-project that demonstrates how to build a complete machine learning pipeline using:

- Infrastructure-as-Code with Terraform
-  ML model training + tracking with scikit-learn and MLflow
-  Multi-platform deployment: AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, Docker, HPC, and GitHub

 Project Purpose
To serve as a portfolio-ready example that shows:
🔧 Provisioning infrastructure using Terraform
🤖 Training and saving a real ML model using Python, scikit-learn, and MLflow
📊 Logging metrics and managing model versions via MLflow
🐳 Containerizing the workflow with Docker
☁️ Demonstrating multi-cloud portability using consistent ML logic.

Use this project to:

Deploy infra with Terraform
Train + track ML models
Serve them with Docker
Learn multi-cloud MLOps principles

projects.name: ChIP‑seq Modular Analysis Pipeline
projects.description:
Built a modular Bash-based ChIP‑seq analysis pipeline for reproducible, resource-conscious analysis of TF and histone mark datasets in mouse or human samples. Fully POSIX-compliant and Conda-free, it follows ENCODE guidelines and runs without workflow engines (e.g., Nextflow).
🐚 Fully Docker-adaptable and written entirely in Bash, the pipeline prioritizes transparency, automation, and reproducibility for ChIP‑seq workflow

🧩 Automatic sample mapping & grouping: A YAML metadata file handles:
• Sample naming
• Biological replicate grouping
• Auto-matching to correct controls (Input, IgG, Mock)
• Setting proper normalization and comparisons automatically — no manual input pairing required

📄 target_peak_rules.yaml: Defines narrow vs. broad peak style for MACS3.
📄 target_peak_rules_HOMER.yaml: Categorizes targets for HOMER peak calling styles using fields like factor_style_targets, histone_style_targets, dnase_style_targets, etc.

🔍 Peak-level QC & replicates: Includes pseudoreplicate generation, IDR (rescue/self-consistency), FRiP scoring, Jaccard overlap, and PBC.

📈 Reports (HTML + PDF) include:
• Spike-in detection summary
• Replicate QC & fingerprint plots
• IDR plots, FRiP scores, overlap stats
• High-confidence peak metrics

🧬 Annotation & enrichment:
• TSS annotation with HOMER
• Local enrichment (no online tools): GO (BP/CC/MF), KEGG, Reactome, g:Profiler via gprofiler2, clusterProfiler, and org.*.eg.db
• Output summary in PRE_POSSIBLE_OUTCOME.tsv showing shared vs. unique gene targets
